slides.title: Onsoo Botanicals: entering the US market in 2027
Executive summary

claims.claim: Onsoo should enter the US in 2027 through Amazon, the only route within the board's limits, and gate the launch on ad cost
The US is worth entering: K-beauty drove 39% of US facial skincare growth, and the Amazon pilot nearly doubled its sales
evidence: K-beauty sales rose 89% in 2021–25, six times other brands' growth
Pilot buyers rebuy at 29% within 90 days, near the 31% peer benchmark

claims.claim: Only Amazon-led fits the board's limits: retail-led breaks the cash cap, and Japan stays small
evidence: Retail-led needs $20.8M by 2030 and cuts 2027 group margin to 4.5%
Japan pays back by 2029 but adds only $7M of revenue in 2030

slides.title: Why the US
K-beauty brands are the growth engine of US facial skincare, capturing 39% of its growth in 2021–25

claims.claim: 38.6% of the category's growth in 2021–25 came from K-beauty brands
evidence: US facial skincare sales, $B: K-beauty brands 1.9 (2021), 2.3, 2.7, 3.1, 3.6 (2025)

claims.claim: K-beauty brands: sales up 89% since 2021, six times the growth of other brands, lifting their share from 9% to 15%
Other brands: still most of the market, but their sales grew only 15% over the four years
For Onsoo: $26M of US sales in 2030 would be under 1% of what K-beauty sold in 2025, so market size is not the limit
evidence: Onsoo 2030 sales from the planning team's Amazon-led volumes (section 2)

claims.claim: A 2026 trade-press figure of $5.2B for the 'US K-beauty market' also counts makeup and hair care; it is not comparable and is not used

slides.title: The Amazon pilot shows real demand, with monthly units nearly doubling in six months and buyers returning at the peer rate

claims.claim: Sales of the same three SKUs rose in every month of the test
First-time buyers rebuy as often as peers in their first US year, though far less than in Korea
evidence: Repeat rate within 90 days: Onsoo, Korea 48%; First-year skincare brands, Amazon US 31%; Onsoo, US pilot 29%

claims.claim: Demand holds at small scale; the 2027 plan needs 1.8 times June's pace, from seven SKUs instead of three
Cross-border seller, three SKUs; ratings 4.5 stars from 2,140 reviews; the top complaint (6% of reviews) was Korean-only label text

slides.title: Which route
Amazon is where US K-beauty buyers shop, and social media is where they find new brands

claims.claim: Amazon already takes the largest share of US K-beauty skincare sales
evidence: Share of sales 2025: Amazon 41%; Specialty beauty retail 27%; Mass retail 14%; Brand websites (DTC) 12%; Other 6%

claims.claim: Buyers shop on Amazon and discover brands on TikTok far more than in stores
evidence: Survey of 1,200 US women aged 18–44, September 2026: Buy K-beauty most often on Amazon 61%; Found their last new brand on TikTok 38%; Buy K-beauty most often at specialty retail 22%; Found their last new brand in a store 17%

slides.title: Why not retail first
At Onsoo's awareness, newcomers sell about 2.6 units per door a week, short of the 4.0 needed to stay on shelf

claims.claim: 1.7x the sell-through Option B assumes, compared with the median for Onsoo's awareness band
evidence: Units per door per week: Above 20% awareness 4.6; Option B plan 4.5; 10–20% awareness 3.5; Below 10% awareness 2.6; Removal threshold, leading retailer 4
Retail analytics firm, 2025, 46 brands; Option B's 4.5 comes from the retailer's deck on successful newcomers only

claims.claim: Below 10% awareness: even the best quarter of these brands sells only 3.4 units, under the removal line
evidence: Onsoo awareness, September 2026: 4% of facial skincare buyers, 9% of K-beauty buyers; both in the lowest band

claims.claim: 10–20%: the CEO's 15% retail trigger sits in this band, and its median of 3.5 also falls short
Option B plan: matches brands above 20% awareness, five times Onsoo's 4% today

slides.title: The Amazon halo behind Option B is unproven, because the 0.71 correlation also fits brands earning doors after winning online

claims.claim: A correlation cannot show which way the effect runs
evidence: 0.7 doors vs. Amazon sales, 30 brands
Retailers invite brands that already sell well online, which produces the same link
Brand size alone can drive both doors and Amazon sales
The memo gives no test that separates these from a halo

claims.claim: The one peer with scale in both channels grew online first
evidence: $30M Saebom US revenue, 2025
Saebom added 300 retail doors only in 2025, after building its Amazon business
Its doors followed its online sales, the reverse of the memo's claim
So the 1.3 times halo in Option B has no measured basis

claims.claim: Buyers find new brands online, not in stores
evidence: 38% found their last new brand on TikTok
Only 17% found their last new brand in a store

slides.title: Making the Amazon route work

evidence: 25%: the planning case assumes ad cost falls as the brand matures; agency data show it rises as brands bid on broader keywords
28%: at the pilot's level the route pays back, but only in 2030, with almost no room for error

slides.title: The CEO's Amazon-first plan is the right route, but five of its settings should change before approval

claims.claim: Ad cost: from 'ACoS falls to 25% as the brand matures' to 'Plan at the pilot's 28%; hold spend if it passes 29%'
evidence: Peers scaling to $20M pay a median 32%

claims.claim: Retail trigger: from 'Amazon above $10M and awareness above 15%' to 'Amazon above $10M and awareness above 20%'
evidence: At 10–20% awareness, the median newcomer sells 3.5 units per door a week, below the 4.0 cut

claims.claim: Labels: from 'Cross-border seller; some units with Korean-only labels' to 'Own US entity, MoCRA registration and English labels at launch'
evidence: Label text drew 6% of pilot reviews, the top complaint

claims.claim: Tariff: from 'Duty fixed at 15%' to 'Plan for 25% until the mid-2027 decision'
evidence: At 25% duty, payback needs ad cost below 27%

claims.claim: 2030 goal: from 'On the way to $40M by 2030' to 'About $26M in 2030, two-thirds of the ambition'
evidence: No modeled route reaches $40M within the board's limits; 2030 units still grow 29%

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: For March 2027: approve Option A (Amazon-led), with about $2.2M at risk before the first gate, and defer Japan; with the ad-cost gate (ACoS at or below 29%) and the $10M and 20% awareness retail triggers. Change five settings of the CEO's plan: plan at the pilot's 28% ACoS and hold spend if it passes 29%; retail trigger at Amazon above $10M and awareness above 20%; own US entity, MoCRA registration and English labels at launch; plan for 25% duty until the mid-2027 decision; target about $26M in 2030.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended route / Within every financial limit, though no route reaches $40M by 2030; pays back by 2030 only if ad cost stays below 28.6% of sales, so approve it with gates

Rejected: Breaks the cap in 2029 and the margin floor in 2027–29; needs $20.8M by 2030 and cuts 2027 group margin to 4.5%; rests on weak assumptions (4.5 units per door vs 2.6 for newcomers; unproven 1.3x Amazon halo); Mooncrest precedent lost an estimated $21M

Safe, but far from the US ambition: adds only $7M of revenue in 2030, under a fifth of the $40M ambition; would use the one major launch management can run in 2027 and delay the US by at least a year; defer Japan
The right route, but five of its settings should change before approval (ad cost, retail trigger, labels, tariff, 2030 goal)

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text with no images. Charts were taken from the extracted series values, and chart shares are shown as percentages (for example 0.41 is written as 41%). The slide 16 waterfall 'base' series is a layout helper, so only the '$ per unit' values were transcribed. On slide 13, the big number reads '0.7', while the title and executive summary say 0.71. On slide 14, the $21M figure sits in the 'Outcome by 2025' column of the table. The visual layout of the slide 20 timeline, meaning which half-year each milestone falls in, did not survive the text extraction.
